passage: Shalini, you said your classmates on the other side are just idiots. Sit, and let me tell you what I once thought. I'm Lalremsiami, and at sixteen I was sure everyone who disagreed with my side in the school debate was stupid, or worse. It felt good, like standing on high ground. It was also lonely: I ate lunch alone and my messages went quiet. Then my teacher paired me with Zothan, from the other side, for a project. He brought tea and asked about my grandmother's weaving before he said a word about politics. I still disagreed with him. But I couldn't call him stupid anymore. I hold my views more gently now.

qa.q: Who did Lalremsiami's teacher pair Lalremsiami with for the project?
qa.a: The teacher paired Lalremsiami with Zothan.

qa.q: Why did contempt feel good to Lalremsiami, and what did it cost?
qa.a: It felt like standing on high ground, but it cost Lalremsiami friendship: lunch alone and quiet messages. 😊

qa.q: What could Shalini try after hearing this?
qa.a: Notice the stereotype of the other side and talk with one real person from it, holding views with some humility.

qa.q: How might Zothan have seen Lalremsiami at the start?
qa.a: Probably as a stiff classmate from the other side, yet Zothan still brought tea and asked about the grandmother's weaving.

grounding: Lalremsiami recalls seeing the other side as stupid, feeling good and lonely, then meeting one real person from that side.

passage:
In Lisbon, the city council vote on the new housing law had split Siddiq's school in two. Siddiq had read everything from his side, watched every video, and by March he thought the other side were either stupid or cruel. It felt good to be certain. It also meant he'd stopped talking to half his class.

Then his Saturday shift at the food bank paired him with Beatriz, who had campaigned for the other side. He almost asked for a different partner.

They packed boxes for three hours. She told him her grandmother had been evicted when a building was sold, and that was why she believed what she did. He told her about his uncle's rent. They argued, but quietly.

On the tram home, Siddiq realised he'd been picturing a cartoon, not a person. Beatriz wasn't stupid or evil. She was scared about the same thing he was, from a different angle.

He still believed his side was right. He just didn't feel quite so sure it was the only reasonable one.

qa.q: Where did Siddiq work on Saturday with Beatriz?
qa.a: Siddiq worked a shift at the food bank with Beatriz.

qa.q: What was Siddiq feeling before he met Beatriz?
qa.a: Siddiq felt certain and a bit superior, which felt good, but also lonely after he stopped talking to half his class.

qa.q: What changed Siddiq's view, and why does it matter?
qa.a: Spending a shift with Beatriz and hearing her grandmother's story showed him a real person, not a stereotype, so he could hold his view with more humility.

qa.q: What was it like for Beatriz to be partnered with Siddiq?
qa.a: Beatriz may also have felt wary at first, but she chose to share her family's story and argue quietly, which suggests she wanted to be understood.

grounding: It shows a teen who starts to see the other side as stupid or evil, feels good but lonely, then meets one real person from that side and holds his view with humility.

passage:
At the debate club in their Indore school, Sachin had a name for the students on the other side of the reservation debate: "the idiots." He said it at lunch. He said it in the club chat. It felt sharp and funny, and for a while everyone on his side laughed.

But he noticed he ate lunch with fewer people every week. And Gautam, who had argued the opposite side in the last round, just stopped talking to him.

One Friday the teacher paired them for the regional competition, arguing the same motion. Sachin groaned.

In the library, Gautam explained his view: his father was the first in the family to finish school, and he'd seen what a chance can change. Sachin argued back. But he couldn't call Gautam an idiot. He wasn't one.

That evening Sachin deleted his joke from the club chat. He still disagreed with Gautam on most of it. But he started saying, "I think," before his opinions again.

qa.q: What did Sachin call students on the other side?
What was Sachin feeling as fewer people ate lunch with him?
qa.a: Sachin felt lonely, noticing that his sharp jokes were costing him friends even though they felt good at first.

qa.q: What did Sachin do that showed more humility?
qa.a: Sachin deleted the joke from the club chat and started saying "I think" before his opinions, while still disagreeing.

qa.q: How might Gautam feel about being called an idiot by a clubmate?
qa.a: Gautam probably felt hurt and disrespected, which is why he stopped talking to Sachin.

grounding: It shows a teen who comes to see the other side of a debate as stupid, feels good but lonely, then works with one real person from that side and holds his view with humility.
